A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same pessimistic-verification work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and added experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original verification experiments on three benchmarks, scaling comparisons, and manual analyses of false negatives.

after.justification: v2 retains original verification results and adds contest problem-solving experiments, subset comparisons, and runtime/API-cost measurements.

M1.justification: Section 3.5 and Figure 6 add an iterative solution-generation, verification, and error-correction workflow, stopping on acceptance or an iteration limit. The three underlying verification algorithms and appendix prompts remain substantively unchanged. The minimum segmentation size explained in v2 was already shown in v1 Figure 2.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual problem-solving evaluation on six IMO 2025 problems and twelve MathArena Apex 2025 problems, extending coverage beyond judging supplied proofs to generating and refining solutions. IMO-GradingBench, Hard2Verify, and QiuZhen-Bench remain.

E2.justification: The reported GPT-5-mini scaling comparison gains vertical-pessimistic curves in v2 Figure 4, absent from v1 Figure 1. The new solving comparison also includes direct generation without verification alongside workflows using pes@12 and prog@4/4. Existing majority-voting, single-pass, and long-CoT comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: v2 introduces final-iteration manual IMO scoring, per-iteration answer-accuracy evaluation on Apex, and cumulative token accounting including verification. It also adds Gemini 3 configurations, full-versus-300-sample IMO-GradingBench evaluation, and runtime measurements under equal concurrency. These substantially extend the evaluation design beyond the retained binary proof-classification protocol.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether the 300-sample subset represents full IMO-GradingBench performance (Table 1) and whether token savings translate into runtime and API-cost savings (Appendix A.1, Table 4). Scaling and false-negative analyses expand, including Gemini 3 Pro Preview. The six detailed appendix cases are retained rather than newly added.

E5.justification: v2 first reports three trials per Apex setting and displays their individual trajectories in Figure 7 to expose variability. v1 provides no comparable repeated-run reporting. This does not establish additional repetitions for the retained verification experiments; confidence intervals and significance tests are not introduced.

E6.justification: New IMO results report totals of 13/42, 17/42, and 22/42 for direct generation, pes@12, and prog@4/4, using 129K, 1,310K, and 985K equivalent tokens respectively (Table 3). These are new comparisons, not cross-version performance gains. GPT-5-mini's reviewed FN counts change from 5 critical/5 minor/3 nonsense to 10/6/4. Apex trajectories, Gemini 3 verification results, extended scaling curves, subset results, and operational efficiency measurements add substantial evidence.

T1.justification: The balanced-F1 definition, verification-check bound, and mathematical reasoning within the six appendix examples remain substantively unchanged. Notation and typesetting differences introduce no new theorem, proof, assumption, or derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion newly claim demonstrated accuracy and efficiency benefits for frontier-model problem solving on IMO 2025 and Apex. Investigating workflow cost inefficiency becomes an explicit contribution, while QiuZhen-Bench curation disappears from the principal contribution list despite the dataset being retained.

C2.justification: v2 develops fixed-granularity token wastage as a mechanism motivating progressive segmentation, treats benchmark annotation problems as a reliability boundary for frontier models, and discusses harmful refinements and possible geometric-intuition limitations in solving. Section 4.2 adds an explicit rigor-versus-efficiency argument for informal verification. Conversely, v1's class-balance qualification of pruning efficiency is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds operational timing/cost and token-accounting information and changes the code link to THUNLP-MT/pverify. It removes the direct dataset link and v1's explicit QiuZhen recipe specifying random selection of 300 problems, GPT-5-mini generation, and GPT-5 progressive@3/6 labeling. Appendix extraction and verification prompts remain substantively unchanged.

R1.justification: Related work expands into informal and formal verification, with substantive discussion of verification costs and additions including DeepSeekMath-V2, DeepSeek-V3.2, Aristotle, and Seed-Prover 1.5. Simple pessimistic verification is explicitly positioned as a mainstream representative baseline, sharpening the emphasis on progressive decomposition. Earlier scoring-bias and self-inconsistency discussion is removed.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, method explanations are reorganized, datasets and metrics are combined, and a preliminary-experiments subsection is introduced. Related work gains subsections, the conclusion is substantially rewritten, and acknowledgements and an impact statement are added. These changes exceed inserting the new experiments.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch from single-column to two-column layout. Separate model-specific efficiency figures become a combined dataset-organized figure with expanded axes and revised styling; benchmark charts are compressed and updated. New subset, solving, and efficiency tables and workflow/Apex figures are added, while retained diagrams and appendix boxes are relocated and reflowed.

improvement.justification: v1 left downstream solving benefits largely prospective and relied on verification labels that its own cases questioned. v2 substantially strengthens the evidence through direct solving tests with contest scoring and answer checks, subset-representativeness checks, and measured runtime/API costs. The small six- and twelve-problem solving sets and loss of QiuZhen reproducibility details limit the gains, but the new evidence addresses an important gap in practical validation.
